name: Alangudi Apatsahayesvarar Temple
deity: Shiva as Apatsahayesvarar, with the Goddess Elavarkuzhali; Guru (Brihaspati) venerated in the Dakshinamurthy form
tradition: Shaiva; a Navagraha Sthalam for Guru (Jupiter) and a Paadal Petra Sthalam of the Tevaram
summary: The Navagraha shrine for Guru (Jupiter), where Shiva is worshipped as Apatsahayesvarar, the Lord who comes to aid in danger. Devotees seek wisdom, marriage, progeny and relief from Guru dosha, especially on the great Guru Peyarchi transit.

sections.history: Alangudi is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams, the shrines hymned in the Tevaram by the Tamil Shaiva saints, which places its devotional standing well before the surviving stone structure. The temple as it stands is of the Chola period, raised in enduring granite and enlarged by later hands who added halls, gateways and subsidiary shrines. Over the centuries it grew into one of the principal Navagraha centres of the Kaveri delta, drawing pilgrims who make the circuit of the nine planetary temples. Here the planet honoured is Guru, or Brihaspati, the preceptor of the gods, and the sanctum of Shiva as the divine teacher Dakshinamurthy remains the heart of its worship.
sections.architecture: Built in the Dravidian idiom of the Chola country, the temple presents a walled enclosure entered through a towered gateway, with the granite sanctum of Apatsahayesvarar at its core. Pillared halls lead the devotee inward past the shrine of the Goddess Elavarkuzhali and the much-revered niche of Dakshinamurthy, the southward-facing form of Shiva as Guru. Stone mandapas, a sacred tank tied to the temple's own legend, and later additions of successive periods frame the older core. The proportions are restrained and devotional rather than grand, in keeping with a temple whose fame rests on its planetary sanctity rather than monumental scale.
sections.legends: The temple's name recalls the churning of the ocean of milk, when the gods and demons drew out the terrible poison halahala that threatened to consume the worlds. In their distress the celestials turned to Shiva, and here he is remembered as the one who came to their aid in that danger, hence Apatsahayesvarar, the Lord who helps in distress. The town's tank is linked to this deliverance. Because Guru is the teacher of the gods, worship at Alangudi is sought for wisdom and learning, for timely marriage, for progeny and prosperity, and for relief from the afflictions of Guru dosha in one's horoscope.
sections.festivals: The supreme occasion is Guru Peyarchi, the transit of Jupiter from one zodiac sign to the next roughly every twelve months, when vast crowds gather for special abhishekam and worship of Dakshinamurthy. Thursday, the day of Guru, is the chief weekly day of veneration, and Pradosham is observed with devotion to Shiva. The temple also keeps its Brahmotsavam, a multi-day festival of processions and ritual, alongside the regular round of abhishekam offered to the form of Guru.
sections.experience: A visit here is quiet and prayerful rather than crowded, except on Thursdays and above all at Guru Peyarchi, when the town fills and long lines form for the darshan of Guru. Devotees light lamps, offer yellow flowers and cloth associated with Jupiter, and stand before Dakshinamurthy to ask for clarity of mind and the removal of obstacles to marriage and family. The atmosphere within the granite halls is cool and hushed, carried by the sound of bells, the scent of camphor, and the murmured recitation of those who have come for the planetary blessing.

visit.timings: Generally open around 6:00 am to 12:30 pm and 4:00 pm to 8:30 pm; hours are extended on Guru Peyarchi and major festival days. Verify locally before travelling.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected; dress conservatively with shoulders and legs covered as a mark of respect.
visit.photography: Photography within the sanctum is generally not permitted; observe posted signs and follow the instructions of temple staff.
visit.gettingThere: Alangudi lies in Thiruvarur district, about 17 km from Kumbakonam and near Needamangalam. Kumbakonam is the nearest hub, with rail connections there and at Thiruvarur; the nearest airport is Tiruchirappalli, around 90 km away.
